Run low, and the pigment fails, so the hair turns white, silver, or gray. (Red hair is his exception — its color comes from an iron-based pigment rather than ordinary melanin.) Phosphorus is part of most proteins, so a high-protein diet raises your phosphorus intake, and the more phosphorus you take in, the more calcium your body needs to balance it. When that demand goes unmet, he says the excess phosphorus can loosen teeth and drive periodontal disease — along with osteoporosis, arthritis and high blood pressure.

When bread is made from unleavened whole-grain flour, that phytic acid latches onto calcium, iron, zinc and other minerals in the gut and lowers their absorption, binding calcium in particular into an insoluble salt the body can't take up. That's the twist he keeps returning to: the same phytate is a required nutrient on one hand and a mineral-robbing dietary negative on the other.

The bran that gets polished off to turn rice white is exactly where the thiamine (vitamin B1) lives, so a diet built on polished white rice slowly starves the body of it. The result is beriberi, a nervous-system disease of weakness, numbness and paralysis — the name is Sinhalese for "I cannot." Because thiamine is the cofactor the body uses to turn carbohydrates into energy, losing it strikes the tissues that run hottest: the nerves, but also the heart, so advanced cases bring congestive heart failure and life-threatening fluid in the lungs.

Wallach traces the proof to the Dutch physician Gerrit Grijns, who showed in 1901 that beriberi is caused by a deficiency — the missing nutrient being the thiamine removed with the bran. He adds the naval evidence: the Japanese ship Riuyo returned in 1883 with 25 sailors dead and 144 more stricken, and in 1884 the naval surgeon Kanekiro Takaki proved a polished-rice diet was the cause by preventing and curing it with a change of diet. The story even named the vitamin — Funk isolated a crystalline substance from rice polishings that cured beriberi, and because it was an amine essential to life he called it a "vital amine," the root of the word "vitamin." Left unchecked, Wallach says a thiamine deficiency reaches all the way to the mind, from mental confusion to the memory loss of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Pica is the body's craving for non-food things (classically dirt) when it's starved of minerals, and Wallach reads it as a signal of a mineral shortfall rather than a behavior problem. He cites Dickens and Ford's finding that 25 percent of children eat dirt, but believes the true rate of mineral-deficiency pica in American kids is far higher — 80 to 100 percent. The catch is that social rules stop children from actually eating dirt, so the same mineral hunger gets redirected: instead of soil they reach for more soft drinks, more juice, more French fries, cookies, cake, and pasta — more calories all around. That excess, in his telling, is what puts on the weight.

Copper is the cofactor for lysyl oxidase — the enzyme that gives blood vessels their tensile strength and builds the strong, elastic fibers in artery walls. His favorite illustration is a flock of turkeys that were dying of ruptured aortic aneurysms; the deaths stopped once copper was doubled in their feed.

Because the same shortage shows up in pigment as well as connective tissue, Wallach points to premature gray, white, or silver hair as the first visible sign of copper deficiency — a clue often worth noticing before the veins are.

His sharpest point is the irony: these hydrogenated oils were once sold by the medical trade as a safe butter substitute meant to prevent hardening of the arteries — yet he says they are now known to be a direct cause of the very arteriosclerosis, plaque buildup and stroke they were supposed to guard against.

The reason traces back to what cobalt actually is inside the body: a single cobalt atom sits at the very center of vitamin B12, so your requirement for cobalt is really a requirement for the finished B12 molecule. That cobalt/B12 pairing does some of the body's most fundamental work — building DNA and RNA, forming red blood cells, and making the myelin that insulates nerves — and, among those jobs, helping the body manufacture the thyroid hormone thyroxine.

This fits Wallach's larger point about the thyroid: he insists it needs far more than iodine. He says the gland requires all 90 essential nutrients to make thyroxin properly. Iodine combines with the amino acid tyrosine to form the hormone, copper is a required cofactor for actually using that iodine, and molybdenum and cobalt round out the supporting cast. For cobalt itself he prefers 250 to 400 micrograms a day, well above the conventional 3-to-4 microgram allowance.

Because sulfur is built structurally into that tissue, running short of it lets the whole framework break down: he says a sulfur deficiency produces osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, degeneration of the cartilage, and weakened tendons and ligaments. The same shortfall, in his telling, feeds the "collagen diseases" like lupus and sickle-cell anemia.

This is why Wallach singles out sulfur for the degenerative kinds of arthritis — the joint wear where the cartilage itself is wasting away — and names it alongside calcium, magnesium, boron and copper as the cluster of mineral deficiencies behind arthritis. His approach is to rebuild the tissue rather than mask the pain: his arthritis protocol feeds the joints cartilage directly — collagen, glucosamine sulfate and chondroitin sulfate — at 1,000 mg three times a day.

Yes — Wallach lists periodontal disease as one of the health problems of vitamin D deficiency, grouping it with osteoporosis, bone spurs and arthritis. Those belong together because of his core view of gum disease: it isn't really a gum problem at all but bone loss in the jaw. The alveolar bone — the bone that anchors each tooth root — dissolves out from under the gums, so the gums recede and the teeth loosen. He calls it, in effect, osteoporosis of the jaw.

Vitamin D is the link. Its job is to absorb, metabolize and properly deposit calcium and phosphorus into the bones and teeth, so when it runs low that jawbone can't be maintained and begins to give way. Wallach calls today's near-universal vitamin D shortage a "physician-caused disease" — the combined result of being told to avoid the sun, wear sunblock and covering clothing, cut dietary cholesterol like egg yolks and dairy, and skip mineral supplements.

Wallach says these diets work partly because animal protein naturally carries iron and phosphorus, and those minerals quiet "pica" — the craving he pins on mineral deficiency, iron in particular. Pica is what drives people to nibble ice, dirt, even lead-paint chips, and, most relevant to weight, high-calorie snack foods; that snack-food version of the craving is what he says actually causes weight gain and obesity. So a high-protein, modest-fat, low-carbohydrate diet works, in his account, partly by feeding the underlying mineral hunger that otherwise makes people binge on empty calories.

But Wallach treats that as only half the story. He argues the real root cause of obesity is mineral deficiency itself — in his own practice he reports overweight patients were mineral-deficient 100 percent of the time, and that roughly 90 percent of obese people overeat and binge because empty-calorie diets set off that mineral-seeking nibbling. His fix is to add a complete plant-derived mineral supplement to the weight program: he says doing so makes the loss more dramatic for everyone and easier to keep off, because it eliminates the cravings, binge-eating and "stand in front of the open refrigerator" munchies that make other diets fail.

Because it's water-soluble and constantly used up, he says it has to be resupplied daily through diet and supplementation, and a shortfall announces itself out in the extremities: burning sensations in the feet and pain in the arms and legs.

Wallach describes the thyroid gland as functioning like a thermostat that sets the body's basal (resting) temperature and overall metabolic rate -- the pace at which you burn fuel and generate heat. When it runs slow, that setting drops: metabolism falls, less body heat gets produced, and you feel cold. Cold intolerance sits right on his list of hypothyroid symptoms, alongside fatigue, weight gain, hair loss and dry skin.

Why the thyroid slows in the first place, in his telling, usually traces back to iodine. The gland combines iodine with the amino acid (protein building block) tyrosine to manufacture thyroxin, the hormone that actually regulates body temperature and metabolism -- so when iodine runs short (something Wallach says is common, especially as people cut their salt intake on their doctors' advice), thyroxin falls and the thermostat is effectively set too low. Fittingly, the home test he points to is temperature itself: a basal body temperature below 98.7 degrees F flags an underactive thyroid.

The reason traces back to how the gland runs. Wallach explains the thyroid concentrates the mineral iodine and combines it with the amino acid tyrosine to manufacture the hormone thyroxin, which sets your general metabolism, heart rate, body temperature and more. When iodine runs low the gland underperforms and hypothyroidism sets in — and he argues intake is usually low to begin with, made worse as people cut their salt on medical advice (copper is a required cofactor for using iodine, so copper-poor soils feed the problem too).

For the cramping and aching legs themselves, Wallach's treatment leans on the minerals muscles need to contract: liquid plant-derived colloidal calcium, magnesium and potassium, plus betaine HCl (a digestive acid) and pancreatic enzymes at 75-200 mg three times a day before meals to help absorb them.

So a shortfall doesn't just weaken bone; it can undercut the very system that makes testosterone.

Wallach describes it as a scarce, non-metallic trace mineral that never turns up pure in nature — you only find it locked into compounds like borax and boric acid — and it wasn't accepted as essential for humans until 1990. Beyond the hormone role, he ties it to bone metabolism and the efficient use of calcium and magnesium.

It sits near the end of a long list (his Table 11-12) that is otherwise dominated by blood-sugar and mood disorders, and that's the key to how he sees it: chromium's main job in the body is glucose control — it's a core part of the glucose tolerance factor (GTF), the thing that makes insulin work. So the same shortage he blames for low blood sugar, type-2 diabetes and elevated cholesterol also, in his account, turns up as reproductive failure.

What makes it matter, in his telling, is how common and how self-inflicted the deficiency is. He cites the USDA's Richard Anderson that 90% of Americans are chromium-deficient, and he points the finger at dietary sugar directly: colas, fruit juices, honey, candy and table sugar flush chromium out through the urine, raising the natural rate of loss by 300% for a full 12 hours. He adds that the deficiency runs deeper when vanadium — the other trace mineral he pairs with chromium for blood-sugar control — is short at the same time.

Wallach reports that in the long-lived Caucasus peoples — who live in simple stone houses without electricity — blood pressure typically runs about 104/72 even at age 100, far below what most of us come to accept as normal in old age.

The point he draws from this is that high blood pressure isn't an inevitable part of aging. He blames hypertension primarily on chronic calcium deficiency rather than on salt, citing McCarron's 1980 finding — backed, he says, by more than 30 later studies — that calcium deficiency causes high blood pressure, and noting that ionized calcium (the active, unbound form in the blood) runs consistently lower in people with untreated hypertension. He rejects the idea that salt is the culprit at all: he points to the Japanese, who eat about 15 grams of salt a day yet, in his telling, have 85 percent less cardiovascular disease and hypertension than Americans. In his framing these long-lived populations keep their pressure low because they stay well-mineralized — every long-lived people on earth eats red meat, poultry, fish, eggs and dairy, he says — so their bodies never run the mineral deficits he ties to high blood pressure.

He says treating TB patients with it sets off an antagonistic reaction against pyridoxine (vitamin B6), effectively working against the vitamin's function, so the body slides into the classic B6-deficiency picture. Among those signs are the nerve-damage ones — peripheral neuritis, meaning inflammation of the peripheral nerves, and ataxia, a loss of steady coordination.

The reason blocking B6 hits the nerves so hard is what the vitamin does. Wallach explains that pyridoxine is converted into pyridoxal phosphate, the working coenzyme behind transamination and much of the body's amino-acid, fat, and nucleic-acid metabolism. Knock that out and the deficiency reaches well beyond the nerves: he also lists depression, nausea and vomiting, seborrheic dermatitis (itchy, scaly skin), lesions of the mouth's mucous membranes, and, at the severe end, seizures and convulsions.

Because eating meat only covers the intake side — actually absorbing that B12 is a separate job, and Wallach says it's the part that usually breaks down. Pulling B12 out of food takes an acid stomach plus a helper protein called "intrinsic factor," and the intrinsic factor is itself acid-dependent. When stomach acid runs low — the stomach's pH drifting toward neutral or alkaline — or when too little intrinsic factor is made, the B12 in your meat passes straight through unabsorbed. Wallach ties that low stomach acid most often to a salt-restricted diet, since salt is the raw material the stomach uses to manufacture its hydrochloric acid.

The absorbing machinery can also be knocked out physically. Surgery on the stomach zones that secrete intrinsic factor (the fundus and cardia), or damage to the ileum in the small intestine from celiac or Crohn's disease, blocks uptake even with plenty of B12 in the diet. Only a strict vegan — no animal products or supplements at all — is short on intake itself. Left uncorrected, the deficiency drives a megaloblastic anemia (oversized, immature red cells) and a progressive demyelinating neuropathy, meaning the myelin insulation is stripped from the nerves. Because the real bottleneck is absorption, Wallach's fixes work around the stomach: a stomach-acid substitute like betaine HCl to reactivate intrinsic factor, or B12 given by injection or under the tongue to bypass the gut entirely.

He traces the practice back a long way: it was originally recorded in the Greek Healing Temples of light and color at Heliopolis, Egypt, and color healing also appears in Ayurvedic and Traditional Chinese medicine.

Beyond relaxing the muscles, meditation raises circulating DHEA — what he calls the "youth hormone" — while lowering cortisol, which he describes as age-inducing. In his framing that hormonal shift supports the body's broader rejuvenating processes, which is why he presents meditation as part of an anti-aging routine rather than a standalone cure for blood pressure.

Wallach pins high blood pressure primarily on chronic calcium deficiency — citing McCarron's 1980 finding, which he says more than 30 later studies backed, that calcium deficiency causes it. He credits them with anti-cancer work on two fronts. First, they help block the creation of carcinogens — cancer-causing chemicals — in the first place. Second, they switch on and support the body's own built-in "detoxification" and defense processes, so it clears threats more effectively.

To see what "blocking the creation of carcinogens" means in his framework, look at how a carcinogen actually gets made: Wallach explains that the nitrites and nitrates used to preserve cured meats like bacon, ham and deli slices are converted, in the acid of the stomach, into nitrosamines — compounds that can in turn become cancer-causing chemicals. Stopping formation like that, before the carcinogen even exists, is the kind of protection he attributes to chocolate's catechins.

He argues gluten isn't really an allergy but a "contact enteritis": the proteins in small grains irritate the gut lining the same way poison ivy irritates skin — no one is truly allergic to poison ivy, yet almost everyone reacts to it. That constant irritation gradually destroys the intestinal villi, the gut-lining structures that absorb your nutrients, until as much as 85-90% of the absorptive surface can be gone. At that point the body starves for nutrients even on a good diet, and the skin — which depends on those nutrients — breaks out. Wallach ties rosacea, dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, and acne all to this malabsorption, which is exactly why he says "you are what you absorb," not just what you eat.

He points to the essential fatty acids as one concrete link: when the damaged gut can't absorb them, that deficiency by itself produces dry, cracked skin, dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea, and acne. So his approach works both ends — remove the irritant with a gluten-free (and often cow's-milk-free) diet, and rebuild what's missing. Wallach's answer is nutritional deficiency, not the germs. He files gum disease alongside scurvy, beriberi and pellagra — a whole class of diseases medicine first pinned on an infectious agent before they turned out to be deficiencies (he adds cardiomyopathy, Bell's palsy and multiple sclerosis to the same list).

What's actually failing, in his telling, isn't gum tissue being invaded — it's bone loss underneath the gums. As that bone recedes, the gum has nothing to anchor it and pulls back. He rejects the standard dental explanation that food particles packing between the teeth and gums are to blame, and offers the animal kingdom as proof: cows, horses, dogs and cats never floss, brush, or use fluoride mouthwash, yet the veterinary profession eliminated periodontal disease in them purely through nutrition. Pellagra is his historical template — once feared as a contagious, insect-borne illness (like malaria or yellow fever), it turned out to be a simple shortage of niacin, vitamin B3, that cleared when eggs and milk were added back to sufferers' diets.

So his treatment is dietary, not antiseptic: correct the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio by dropping phosphate-laden soft drinks, then supplement calcium at 2,000 mg and magnesium at 1,000 mg a day.

Yes — Wallach lists gray hair as one of the early signs of a strict vegan diet. His reasoning is about minerals, not vitamins: plants can't manufacture minerals, so a diet built entirely on plants leaves the body short of them — by his count, an unsupplemented vegan runs 51 to 57 of the body's essential minerals short. Because most vegans don't supplement heavily and correctly with a special emphasis on minerals, he says the shortfall shows on the body within about five years.

In his telling gray hair rarely comes alone — he groups it with a whole cluster of deficiency signs that surface in the same window: receding gums and periodontal disease, anemia, osteoporosis and arthritis, hypertension, blood sugar problems, chronic fatigue, and in the worst cases even cancer and liver cirrhosis. Wallach rejects the vegan premise outright, arguing that every long-lived population on earth eats animal foods — red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy — and pointing to vegan crusader Linda McCartney, who he says died at 56 of breast cancer.

Besides calcium, Wallach reaches for magnesium, boron, copper, sulfur, selenium, and strontium. He treats restless leg the same way he treats osteoporosis, which in his framework is fundamentally a calcium-deficiency disease: when the diet runs chronically short of calcium, the body pulls it back out of the bones to keep blood levels steady, thinning the skeleton. But calcium can't do the job alone — Wallach says holding and building bone depends on those co-factor minerals alongside it, which is why his formula corrects all of them together rather than just handing you calcium.

The other half of his approach is cutting what works against those minerals: excess phosphorus (which he says raises the body's calcium requirement), fluoride, cadmium, dietary fats, and salt. And the pattern isn't unique to restless leg — Wallach applies the very same six-mineral cluster, plus the same cut in excess phosphorus and dietary fat, to sciatica, another lower-body complaint he files under calcium-deficiency low-back problems.

The mechanism he points to is damage to the gut lining. He calls the broader pattern the "Feedlot Syndrome" — people put on a mineral-depleted diet, stripped of their traditional "culinary" and garden ashes, gain weight unless they consciously supplement with plant minerals.

The mirror image, in his account, is the Old Order Amish: they eat more sugar, fat, red meat and dairy than almost anyone, yet their obesity rate runs about 4% and their type-II diabetes rate about 6% — roughly a tenth and a half, respectively, of their modern neighbors in the very same county. He credits that gap not to their diet, nor even to their farm labor, but to the essential minerals in the wood ashes they spread on their garden soil every morning — the same minerals the urban Navajo gave up.

The deeper reason he'd steer you away from painkillers is that, in his framework, the pain has a nutritional root. Wallach lists premenstrual syndrome among the diseases he traces to calcium deficiency — one of no fewer than 147 conditions he attributes to a calcium deficiency or imbalance — so his instinct is to correct the shortfall rather than numb the symptom. He also recounts an older, gentler route to the same relief: Lydia Pinkham's herbal compound, built on an ancient Native American recipe and marketed for PMS and dysmenorrhea (painful periods), which worked so well it made her an American icon.

In Wallach's framework, yes -- but he'd say the trouble isn't really in your skin. Yes — and Wallach's evidence is one of nutrition's classic experiments, McCarrison's rat-feeding study. One group of rat pups was raised on a typical working-class English diet of the day: white bread, margarine, sugared tea, boiled vegetables, canned meat and cheap jams — plenty of food, but stripped of real nourishment. Those rats didn't just fall physically ill (McCarrison logged diseases of the lungs, stomach, intestines and nerves); they turned mean. They grew nervous, bit the attendants who fed them, lived unhappily crowded together, and by the sixteenth day began killing and eating the weaker animals in the cage.

The force of the picture comes from the comparison group in the same experiment. Those rats ate a Hunza-style diet — whole-grain flatbread, butter, legumes, raw carrots and cabbage, whole milk, eggs, meat and daily sunlight — and stayed calm, with no aggression and no early deaths, reaching 27 months of age (the equivalent of 55 human years) free of overt disease. For Wallach the takeaway is blunt: the only thing that differed was what went in the food bowl, so the nervousness, bad temper and even violence trace straight back to the diet of processed junk.

Yes. Wallach describes exactly that from ergot poisoning, the toxin a grain fungus produces. Two of its signature signs are paresthesia — itching and prickling — and formication, the unnerving feeling that ants are crawling under the skin. Those sit inside a much larger symptom storm he lists: painful seizures and spasms, diarrhea, vomiting, headaches, vertigo, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), and mind-level effects like mania, psychosis, and hallucinations.

The gravest damage, though, is circulatory rather than sensory. The fungus's alkaloids — ergotamine and ergocristine — drive vasoconstriction, a hard clamping-down of the blood vessels. Starve the fingers and toes of blood long enough and the tissue dies, producing dry gangrene in the extremities.

That crawling-skin feeling isn't unique to poisoning, either. Wallach ties the same paresthesia, especially in the hands and feet, to a biotin deficiency — showing up there alongside hair loss, skin lesions around the nose and mouth, and depression.
